errors.english: to refute those who would harm the self [note: by asserting its existence], the following logical consequence was stated
errors.why: The consequence that follows (no beings, so no object of compassion) is the opponent's objection against selflessness, stated in order to be refuted; the note casting the 'harmers' as those who assert a self inverts who is objecting.

note: A faithful rendering of the argument that past, future and present minds can't be the self, and of the plantain simile; only the final transitional note is misleading.

errors.english: The actions of the Supreme Sage
errors.why: MMK 17.2 (karmoktaṃ paramarṣiṇā): the Supreme Sage taught that actions are intention and intended; these are not the Sage's own actions, as the commentary's gloss on the Sage as the teacher confirms.

fix.find: The actions of the Supreme Sage

note: Sound rendering of Avalokitavrata on cetanā/cetayitvā; only the root verse's agent is misconstrued.

errors.english: it is pervaded by one portion of the direction of the property of the (subject) dharmin that is to be proven
errors.why: ཕྱོགས here is pakṣa (the thesis), not 'direction', and the sentence says the property of the subject is pervaded by a portion of the pakṣa.

fix.find: it is pervaded by one portion of the direction of the property of the (subject) dharmin that is to be proven
fix.replace: the property of the (subject) dharmin that is to be proven is pervaded by one portion of the thesis (pakṣa)

errors.english: Furthermore, since these are of a nature that exists in all things, such a distinction is impossible.
errors.why: These are two separate reasons: anvaya/vyatireka are by nature present in all instances, and that (all-presence) is impossible in a particular. The English merges them into 'such a distinction is impossible'.

errors.english: the presence of the reason where the predicate is present, and its absence where the predicate is absent
errors.why: Anvaya is the presence of the predicate wherever the reason is present (or the reason's occurrence only in similar instances), not the reason's presence wherever the predicate is present; as written, the note misdefines pervasion.

errors.english: In order to understand the pervader, it is appropriate to understand the qualified itself.
errors.why: The Tibetan says the qualified (the reason) is properly the means of making known (gamaka) with respect to the pervader, which is what is to be made known; the gamaka role is lost.

note: The overall line of the argument on restriction (avadhāraṇa) in the pervasion clause survives, but the key pakṣa term and two logical relations are garbled.

errors.english: If that identity [note: original: "tādātmya"]
errors.why: The side's opening line is untranslated: the ascertainment as arising from that is uncertain, and since it is occasional the capacity to make known is uncertain; then the question of why, if the reason is uncertain, the capacity must be so too, answered by the lemma 'If'.

fix.replace: The certainty of being arisen from that is uncertain; since it exists only occasionally, the capacity to make known is uncertain. If one asks, "From what does it follow that if the reason is uncertain, the capacity to make known must be likewise?"—the answer is "If...": For if that identity [note: original: "tādātmya"]

note: Apart from the dropped opening line, the rest of the passage on saṃyoga and the possessor as a reason is rendered adequately.

errors.english: somewhat heavy [mud]
errors.why: ལྕི་བ here is cow dung (gomaya), the stock heterogeneous cause from which a plant is seen to arise; it does not mean 'heavy'.

errors.english: Otherwise, there would sometimes be no meaning at all.
errors.why: The sense is that otherwise the thing (smoke) would not occur even once; it is not 'sometimes no meaning'.

errors.english: in order to ascertain the object and time
errors.why: This says 'because of the restriction to place and time': ཡུལ is place, and ཕྱིར gives the reason, not a purpose.

note: The svavṛtti on the smoke–fire nature and the anthill (śakramūrdhan) verses is correctly identified, but several glosses on the Indian examples are wrong.

errors.english: # Whatever the nature of destruction is
errors.why: The lemma continues རྒྱུན་ཆད་ from the previous side: 'whatever is of the nature of the cutting off of the continuum'. It is not a generic 'destruction', and it is a cited verse phrase, not a heading.

errors.english: when we later explain the destruction of a pot and so forth
errors.why: འཆད་པར་འགྱུར་བ here means a pot etc. being cut off (ceasing), glossed as 'that very thing does not arise'; it does not mean 'we will explain'.

note: A generally reliable rendering of the two kinds of destruction and the diminishing-cause account of contradiction.

errors.english: the head of Indra [note: referring to a traditional example of something that is not fire, such as a cold or divine object]
errors.why: བརྒྱ་བྱིན་གྱི་སྤྱི་བོ renders śakramūrdhan, 'anthill', the stock example in Dharmakīrti's verse; it is not Indra's head, and the note invents a 'cold or divine object'.

fix.find: the head of Indra [note: referring to a traditional example of something that is not fire, such as a cold or divine object]

errors.english: then that [note: the head] would become the cause, fire
errors.why: Following the verse (འབྱུང་ན་དེ་ནི་རྒྱུ་མེད་འགྱུར), the consequence is that the smoke would be causeless; it is not the anthill becoming the cause, fire.

errors.english: for we accept such a distinction between fire and smoke, but not for fire in general
errors.why: This says that a particular kind of fire and smoke is accepted as such, not fire as such; it is not a 'distinction between fire and smoke'.

errors.english: fire does not transcend being a benefactor [note: a cause] and performing the act of benefiting [note: producing an effect]
errors.why: The pair is upakārya and upakāraka, 'what is benefited and what benefits', a relation between two relata; it is not two activities of fire.

note: The dialectic on fire as a cause of smoke can be followed, but the stock anthill example is mistranslated along with its consequence, and several technical pairs are misread.

errors.english: How does a certain hundred know that
errors.why: བརྒྱ་ཞིག་ལ/ན is the idiom 'perchance, if by chance'; it has nothing to do with 'a hundred'.

fix.find: How does a certain hundred know that
fix.replace: How, pray, is it known that

errors.english: That is not so: if this has parts, it would not become substantially existent.
errors.why: Here དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ means 'otherwise', supporting the preceding claim that it must be partless; it is not a rejection of that claim.

note: A sound rendering of the argument that atoms admit no differences of shape, apart from one idiom and one connective.

errors.english: One cannot refute direct perception because one cannot refute an inference (anumāna) logical deduction that arises from a mark characterized by the three modes of proof
errors.why: The Tibetan says that without refuting perception one cannot refute an inference born of a mark whose three modes are established by perception; the English inverts the dependency and drops 'established by it'.

fix.find: One cannot refute direct perception because one cannot refute an inference (anumāna) logical deduction that arises from a mark characterized by the three modes of proof
fix.replace: For without refuting direct perception, one cannot refute an inference (anumāna) that arises from a mark characterized by the three modes established by it

errors.english: it becomes faint.
errors.why: This completes the previous side's སྲིད་པ་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པ་ཁོ་ནར་འགྱུར་རོ, 'existence would be utterly without nature'; 'becomes faint' has no basis.

errors.english: a person like Maitreya
errors.why: In this stock example, བྱམས་པ is Maitra, the generic person of Indian logical examples (like Devadatta), not the bodhisattva Maitreya.

note: The argument about recognition, conceptual superimposition and perception is partly traceable, but a key dependency is inverted and some terms are misread.

errors.english: At the conclusion of the speech,
errors.why: This means 'while the cry [of the gods' 'well done, O king!'] was travelling to the ends of the directions' (nṛpa sādhuvāde); it is not the end of a speech.

note: The verse is rendered competently and the Sanskrit is properly set off in notes; only the opening circumstance is misread.
